newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan needs $3 bln for July-December payments.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan needs $3 bln for July-December payments.

text.p: Pakistan will require about $3.0 billion during July to December for external payments, analysts said on Saturday.
Pakistan had a funding capability of $1.65 billion without the International Monetary Fund (IMF) support and would break even with IMF support, analyst Kalim Aziz of Ing Barings said.

"We continue to forecast an external payment requirement of about $3.0 billion during July to December 1997 and funding capability of about $1,650 million without IMF support and breaking even with the IMF support," Aziz said in his latest report.

The next period for debt servicing and repayment pressure for Pakistan was expected in September 1997, and therefore it was essential that Pakistan had some form of support from the IMF to ride it through the year, Aziz said.

"Debt repayment of about $600 million was made in the month of March," Aziz said. Even after the repayment of debt and funding of the current account deficit, the reserves declined to $730 million, indicating an inflow of $450 million during March.
He said: "We continue to forecast $200 million per month of current account deficit for the last quarter of financial year 1996/97."
However, the Ing Barings forecast for the last month of the current year is revised upwards to $950 million (rollover of March added to original payments), he said.
On the funding side, the analyst has changed the Pakistan Telecommunication Company Ltd (PTCL) amount, the National Debt Retirement Scheme (NDRS) and the roll over estimates.

"The PTCL receivable estimate of $80 million represents the amount still to be arranged against the receivable securitisation (the total commitment was $200 million, of which about $115 million has been bridge financed by ABN-AMRO)," Aziz said.

The roll over figures are revised upwards on the back of recent experience, he said. "So far $171 million has been raised under the NDRS effort. We expect about another $80 million under this head, raising the total to $250 million."
Another analyst said the IMF mission was likely to visit Pakistan in May as a follow-up to the economic package announced by Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz on March 28.
"The mission will conduct a technical appraisal of the economic package and its outcome," he said, adding: "The mission is not visiting Pakistan to negotiate any funding proposition."
Aziz said the mission's visit during the preparation of the 1997/98 federal budget would lead to a conclusion that the IMF was being consulted on budgetary measures.
Pakistan went for growth in a high-risk strategy that could pay off if the government can weather a short-term financial crisis, one banker said.
The government introduced bold reforms, including tax and tariff cuts to revive growth and stimulate exports saying the IMF had agreed to negotiate a medium-term loan later this year.
